To separate the remaining top models (M20, M14, M11, M18), we must exploit their differing reaction orders with respect to the catalyst and their dependencies on the substrate. 
All previous experiments used relatively high catalyst concentrations (0.1 to 0.2). By running an experiment with a low catalyst concentration (cat=0.01), we can cleanly isolate M18. Because M18 involves bimolecular catalyst deactivation (2catS -> inactive), its deactivation rate will plummet by a factor of 100 relative to the first-order deactivation models (M14, M11, M20). If M18 is the true model, the catalyst will appear vastly more stable in this run.
Furthermore, by using a lower substrate concentration (S=0.5), we shift the equilibrium to increase the proportion of free `cat` relative to the `catS` complex. This will strongly differentiate M20 from M14 and M11. M20 deactivates via both free `cat` and `catS`, so it will maintain a high deactivation rate even as `catS` decreases. In contrast, M14 relies entirely on `catS` for deactivation, and M11 relies on the product of [S] and [cat], both of which will decrease at lower substrate levels.
</hypothesis>
